strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-examined problem: the validity of standard random-sampling evaluation protocols in class incremental learning.

It provides a systematic empirical demonstration that using only a few random class sequences can bias mean estimates, underestimate variance, and miss performance extremes, especially on controlled enumerable settings.
The proposed EDGE protocol is simple, practical, and leverages pre-trained CLIP text embeddings to identify semantically similar classes, requiring no image access.

The empirical study includes both non-pre-trained and pre-trained CIL methods and reports distributional metrics (JSD, Wasserstein distance) that are appropriate for comparing estimated and ground-truth distributions.
The theoretical analysis, while not flawless, attempts to formalize why random sampling is inefficient and why extreme sequences can reduce sample complexity.
weaknesses: The core EDGE protocol uses only three sequences (hard, easy, and one random) to estimate a full performance distribution. This is statistically unsound: including two deliberately extreme sequences with equal weight strongly biases the sample mean and variance. The theoretical justification in Theorem 2 explicitly requires L additional random samples and a large L to make the extreme sequences' influence negligible; EDGE instead uses L=1 and does not correct for this bias.

The theoretical results do not adequately support the proposed protocol. Theorem 2's proof incorrectly sets Z_0 = μ despite deterministically including extreme sequences, so the martingale argument ignores the bias term. Lemma 1 also contains asymptotic inaccuracies regarding |Ω| when K = Θ(N), and Theorem 1 is misinterpreted as implying that a random sequence lies near the median.

The empirical validation is very narrow: the main quantitative study uses only the first six classes from CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-R, with three tasks of two classes each (90 sequences). This is far from standard CIL benchmarks and may not reflect behavior in realistic settings with more classes, tasks, and complex class semantics. The classic CIL experiments in Figure 5 lack ground-truth distributions and only show estimated min/max bounds, so they cannot validate the central claim of more accurate distributional approximation.

The reliance on inter-task similarity is weakly supported. Reported Pearson correlations in Figure 2c are low (e.g., 0.11–0.37), meaning semantic similarity explains little variance in model performance. Consequently, similarity-based hard/easy sequence construction may fail to identify true performance extremes, as seen in several cases where EDGE still misses the ground-truth upper bound by a large margin.

The paper does not compare against alternative evaluation protocols, such as stratified sampling, importance sampling, more random samples, or sampling based on model features. It only compares to a 3-sequence random-sampling baseline, so it is unclear whether EDGE is better than simply increasing the number of random sequences.

Reproducibility details are insufficient: the CLIP text prompt templates, hierarchical clustering linkage and granularity search set, and exact procedure for fitting Gaussian estimates from the three EDGE sequences are not specified. The code is promised but not provided in the submitted manuscript.

Several citations are inaccurate (e.g., ImageNet-R is repeatedly cited as [15], which is the CIFAR reference), and some claims are stronger than the evidence, such as 'consistently achieves both a lower estimated lower bound and a higher upper bound across nearly all scenarios.'

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored issue: class-order sensitivity and under-sampling in CIL evaluation.
Conducts small-scale exhaustive experiments on 6 classes/3 tasks to compare distributions via JSD and Wasserstein distance.
Proposes EDGE, a simple and intuitive protocol that uses CLIP text embeddings and inter-task similarity to construct easy/hard sequences.
Reports empirical gains: EDGE often gives closer lower/upper bounds and lower JSD/Wasserstein distances than the standard 3-seed RS protocol on the enumerable setting.
Provides pseudo-code and some algorithmic details for extreme sequence generation.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is technically flawed. Theorem 1 bounds the sample mean using a union bound over |Ω| sequences and includes log |Ω| in the sample complexity, which is incorrect for estimating a single population mean; standard Hoeffding/Azuma bounds for bounded random variables do not require this.

Theorem 2 and Theorem 3 are hand-wavy and rely on strong, unstated assumptions. Theorem 3 in particular imports a prior generalization-error lemma and assumes CLIP text similarity is equivalent to representation-space similarity, which is not justified.

The enumerable evaluation is far too limited: only the first six classes of CIFAR-100/ImageNet-R, split into three tasks of two classes. This is not representative of standard CIL benchmarks and cannot support broad claims about the true performance distribution.

In the classic CIL setting, there is no ground-truth distribution; the paper only shows that EDGE captures wider min/max bounds, not that these bounds are more accurate. This is insufficient to validate the central claim that EDGE better approximates the true distribution.

The only baseline is the standard RS protocol with three seeds. There is no comparison to other sampling strategies, to RS with more random seeds, or to model-specific extreme-sequence search, so the benefit of EDGE over simpler alternatives is unclear.

EDGE relies entirely on CLIP text embeddings to define class similarity, but no evidence shows that text similarity aligns with the visual representation space of the CIL models. The generated hard/easy sequences may not be true extremes across architectures and datasets.

Estimating a full distribution from only three sequences is inherently crude. Fitting a Gaussian and reporting JSD/Wasserstein from three points is unstable, and the paper does not ablate the number of sampled sequences.

Some claims are overreaching. For example, the paper states that RS produces biased mean estimates and severely underestimates variance, but the theoretical support for the mean-estimation claim is not rigorous, and the distributional guarantee for EDGE is not established.

Novelty is limited: order sensitivity in CIL and similarity-based task ordering are known, and the proposed contribution is mostly a heuristic evaluation protocol without strong theoretical or empirical validation.
Reproducibility is weakened by a missing/empty code link and missing details in the main text, with several important analyses relegated to an appendix containing typos and unclear notation.

strengths: Identifies an important and underexplored problem in CIL: standard random-sampling evaluation with only a few sequences yields biased mean estimates, severely underestimates variance, and misses performance extremes.
Provides theoretical analysis of the combinatorial explosion of class sequences and sample-complexity arguments that motivate the need for extreme-case sampling rather than purely random sampling.

Proposes EDGE, a practical evaluation protocol that uses CLIP text embeddings, hierarchical clustering, and greedy sequence construction to identify hard, easy, and median class sequences based on inter-task similarity.

Conducts extensive experiments across enumerable settings and classic CIL benchmarks with many non-pre-trained and pre-trained CIL methods, showing that EDGE often better approximates the ground-truth distribution and captures extreme performance bounds; code is available.
weaknesses: The theoretical foundations are not fully rigorous: Theorem 2 uses R^(sigma)=A(omega+)-A(omega-) as a sensitivity range even though sampled sequences may fall outside this range, and Theorems 3-4 rely on strong assumptions and somewhat hand-wavy derivations rather than providing clean guarantees for EDGE.

EDGE estimates the full performance distribution from only three sequences (hard, median, easy). Fitting a Gaussian from three points is statistically unstable and may introduce its own bias, and there is no formal convergence or distribution-estimation guarantee that the resulting estimate matches the true distribution.

Extreme sequences are generated using CLIP text similarity as a proxy for model difficulty. The positive correlation between inter-task similarity and accuracy is empirical and not universal, so EDGE may fail when actual difficulty is driven by visual or domain-specific factors not reflected in class-label semantics.

The enumerable ground-truth experiments are limited to 6 classes and 3 tasks; in the classic CIL settings, there is no ground-truth distribution, so distribution-level advantages are not fully verified, and some results show EDGE is not uniformly better (e.g., L2P on ImageNet-R has worse Wasserstein distance under EDGE than RS).

The baseline comparison focuses on the RS protocol only. There is no comparison to other robust sampling or active evaluation strategies, and no ablation on the number of sampled sequences or detailed sensitivity analysis beyond scaling the CLIP text encoder.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: evaluation protocols for class incremental learning, especially sensitivity to class-arrival order and the inadequacy of only averaging a few random sequences.
Provides a small-scale but fully enumerable ground-truth study (6 classes, 3 tasks, 90 sequences) that directly demonstrates RS can produce biased mean estimates and severely underestimate variance.
Proposes a concrete and simple evaluation protocol, EDGE, which uses CLIP text embeddings and inter-task similarity to construct hard and easy class sequences without accessing image instances.
Reports experiments across multiple CIL methods, datasets, distribution metrics (JSD/Wasserstein), model-ranking analyses, and robustness checks to different backbones and CLIP encoder scales.
Includes additional baselines (LLM-generated sequences, adversarial sampling, max-cover sampling) in the appendix, which helps position EDGE against possible alternatives.
Makes a reasonable effort toward reproducibility by integrating EDGE into two CIL toolboxes and providing run instructions, although key links/details are incomplete.
weaknesses: Major theoretical flaw in Theorem 1: the sample-complexity bound unnecessarily includes a union bound over all |Ω| sequences, yielding a log|Ω| factor. For estimating the mean with bounded accuracy, standard Hoeffding/Azuma bounds give O(1/ε^2) samples independent of |Ω|, not O(N log N / ε^2). Thus the central claim that random sampling is fundamentally impractical because of combinatorial explosion is not supported.

Theorem 2 has a serious bias issue: the proposed estimator that includes two extreme sequences is not unbiased for the true mean unless the two extremes are symmetric around μ. The proof applies a concentration bound around μ without accounting for this bias, so the claimed sample-size reduction is not rigorously justified.

Theorem 3 is only loosely connected to general CIL: its proof relies on a specific linear overparameterized model and several informal proportionality arguments (e.g., Eq. 35–36), rather than a rigorous derivation applicable to arbitrary CIL methods. The similarity–generalization relationship is mostly empirically observed, not theoretically established.

Theorem 4's greedy-strategy optimality bound appears unsound: the argument uses informal order-statistic and union-bound reasoning (e.g., bounding Δ_t by twice its mean) and does not establish the stated high-probability guarantee in a rigorous way.

EDGE itself approximates the performance distribution using only three deterministic sequences (hard, easy, random) and then fits a Gaussian via mean/std. With three samples, the variance estimate is extremely unreliable, so calling it a faithful approximation of the full distribution is an overstatement.
The enumerable evaluation is very small-scale (first six classes, 90 sequences). While useful as a sanity check, it may not generalize to realistic CIL settings with many classes and tasks.

The large-scale experiments lack ground-truth distributions, so claims that EDGE captures true extremes are not independently verified. The comparison mainly shows that EDGE's similarity-guided sequences tend to yield lower/higher accuracies than random sampling, which is partly expected if inter-task similarity correlates with difficulty.

The main text compares EDGE against RS using only three samples each; the more thorough comparison against larger RS budgets is relegated to the appendix, and the practical advantage of EDGE over simply using more random sequences is not fully established in the main paper.

Novelty is moderate: order sensitivity and task similarity in CIL are already known, and constructing easy/hard sequences by clustering CLIP text embeddings is a relatively straightforward heuristic. The distributional-evaluation framing is interesting, but the technical contribution is not clearly strong enough for a top-tier venue.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link is blank/anonymous in the manuscript, and some algorithmic details are inconsistent (e.g., Algorithm 2 uses the similarity matrix D in an unusual way, and notation/definitions vary).

Claims are stronger than the evidence: the title and abstract suggest a definitive expose and a reliable full-distribution estimator, but the theoretical results are flawed and the empirical validation is limited to small enumerable settings plus unverified large-scale heuristics.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored issue: the reliability of evaluation protocols in class incremental learning, especially the mismatch between a few random class orders and the full sequence distribution.

Provides a clear critique of the common random-sampling (RS) protocol, showing empirically that a small number of random sequences can yield biased mean/variance estimates and misleading model rankings.

Proposes an evaluation framework, EDGE, that attempts to construct easy, medium, and hard task orders using class semantic similarity, offering a practical alternative to purely random sequence sampling.
Uses CLIP text embeddings to avoid requiring access to image instances when constructing task orders, which is a reasonable practical choice for a dataset-level evaluation protocol.
Includes enumerable small-scale experiments where the ground-truth distribution is known, which is an appropriate way to quantitatively test an evaluation protocol when full enumeration is feasible.
Reports additional analyses and baselines in the appendix, provides open-source code, and discusses reproducibility resources.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is weak and in places appears technically flawed. Lemma 1 is a standard combinatorial count, Theorem 1 uses a very loose union bound over all sequences and yields impractical sample complexity, and Theorem 2 assumes access to known extreme sequences whose values bound the entire range; the proof also implicitly treats these as min/max sequences, which is not stated or justified.

Theorem 3, which is central to the motivation for using inter-task similarity, is not rigorously proven. It relies on strong and unclear assumptions, manipulates an upper bound from prior work without carefully connecting it to actual expected generalization error, and does not establish the claimed ordering of generalization errors for arbitrary CIL methods.

The key assumption that inter-task similarity predicts model performance is only weakly supported empirically. Figure 2c shows weak correlations for several methods (e.g., iCaRL, Hide-Prompt, L2P), yet EDGE relies on this assumption to construct performance extremes. There is no guarantee that similarity-generated hard/easy sequences correspond to true worst/best-case sequences.

The main evaluation is too limited to support the broad claims. Ground-truth distribution evaluation is only possible on a 6-class/3-task subset, which is far from standard CIL benchmarks. In the larger CIL settings, no ground-truth distribution is available, so the experiments only show that EDGE finds more extreme sampled accuracies, which is largely expected by construction rather than evidence of more accurate distribution estimation.

Baselines are insufficient. The main tables compare EDGE mostly against RS, while alternative sequence-generation strategies appear only in the appendix and are not integrated into the primary quantitative comparison. There is also no comparison to other recent evaluation protocols or benchmarks for CIL robustness and distributional assessment.

The claim that EDGE captures the full performance distribution is overstated. EDGE evaluates only three sequences, so it provides heuristic boundary estimates at best, not a characterization of the entire distribution. Similarly, the claim that a random median sequence is 'theoretically guaranteed' to lie near the center is false for a single sample; Theorem 1 gives an average-case concentration statement, not a deterministic guarantee.

CLIP text similarity is an indirect proxy for visual difficulty. The paper provides only limited validation that this proxy aligns with image-space similarity, and the authors themselves note failures in medical/professional domains. Since the method constructs extreme sequences from class labels, its reliability depends heavily on the quality of these text embeddings, which is not adequately established for the main benchmarks.

EDGE has several sensitive design choices, including the choice of CLIP encoder, clustering granularity, hierarchical clustering procedure, and greedy sequence construction. The paper does not provide sufficient ablation or sensitivity analysis to show that the protocol is robust to these choices.

Some empirical results contradict the central narrative: for example, on CIFAR-100 DER has a worse lower-bound estimate under EDGE than under RS, and several methods show only small or no improvements. The paper tends to report qualitative conclusions without statistical significance tests or confidence intervals for the distributional metrics.

The novelty is limited relative to prior work on CIL evaluation and robustness. Critiques of simplistic evaluation are not new, and EDGE combines existing components (CLIP embeddings, clustering, greedy similarity-based ordering) without a sufficiently rigorous new theoretical or empirical foundation.

Reproducibility and comparability for the large-scale experiments are unclear: the experimental protocol changes class subsets, methods, and evaluation settings, but it is not always clear whether all methods were trained under identical, standard conditions or whether the reported gains come from the evaluation protocol rather than re-implementation differences.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: evaluation protocols for class incremental learning, showing that standard random sampling of a few class orders can miss extreme sequences and give an incomplete picture of model robustness.

Provides an extensive empirical study, including fully enumerable small-scale experiments on CIFAR-100/ImageNet-R, comparisons across many pre-trained and non-pre-trained CIL methods, and additional analyses of model rankings, sample efficiency, and alternative baselines.

Proposes EDGE, a simple and computationally practical protocol that constructs hard/easy/median sequences using CLIP text embeddings and inter-task similarity; the method is easy to integrate into existing CIL toolboxes.
Includes useful ablations/robustness checks (different backbones, CLIP encoder sizes, LLM and adversarial baselines) and a reproducibility statement with code integration details.

Demonstrates that EDGE often estimates performance bounds and distributional distances closer to ground truth than the standard 3-seed RS protocol, supporting the practical value of similarity-guided extreme-sequence sampling.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis of RS has a significant issue: Theorem 1 estimates the mean accuracy over all sequences, but the proof uses an unnecessary union bound over all |Ω| sequences, introducing a ln|Ω| factor. For estimating a population mean under uniform sampling, standard Hoeffding/Azuma bounds do not require this factor, so the claimed exponential sample complexity for mean estimation is not justified. Moreover, the sample mean from random sampling is unbiased for the population mean; the paper's framing of RS as producing 'biased mean estimates' is stronger than the evidence supports (the observed bias is due to particular random seeds/small samples, not a systematic bias of the estimator).

The central theoretical support for EDGE (Theorem 2) assumes access to true extreme sequences satisfying A(omega+) - mu >= sigma and mu - A(omega-) >= sigma. EDGE only constructs sequences via semantic similarity and provides no guarantee that these assumptions hold. In several results, EDGE's hard/easy estimates do not reach the true minimum/maximum, so the theorem does not directly justify the practical algorithm.

The similarity-to-generalization relation (Theorem 3) is argued under strong, model-specific assumptions (e.g., overparameterized linear model intuition) and a loose concentration argument. The empirical correlation between inter-task similarity and accuracy is suggestive but does not establish that CLIP text similarity reliably identifies the true hardest/easiest sequences across models and domains.

EDGE estimates a performance distribution from only three sequences (hard, median, easy). It is unclear how these three points are used to fit or approximate a Gaussian distribution, and this crude estimate may be unstable. The paper reports JSD/Wasserstein distances but does not fully specify the estimation procedure or provide uncertainty quantification for the estimated distribution.

The main empirical validation of distribution approximation is limited to an enumerable setting with only 6 classes and 3 tasks (90 sequences), which may not reflect larger-scale CIL. The classic CIL experiments lack ground-truth distributions, so they mainly show that EDGE captures more extreme bounds, not that it better estimates the true distribution.

CLIP text embeddings of bare class names may not reflect visual similarity in fine-grained or specialized domains. The appendix itself shows weak agreement on medical datasets unless class names are expanded with LLM-generated visual captions, but this augmentation is not integrated into the main EDGE protocol, limiting claims of general robustness.

Although EDGE is compared to several auxiliary baselines in the appendix, the primary comparison is still against a 3-random-seed RS protocol. Since EDGE uses additional side information (CLIP embeddings, clustering/search) and extra computation, the comparison is not fully cost-matched. There is also little statistical significance testing across seeds/datasets.
